newsitem.title: USA: Online bookstore war seen as Barnes & Noble enters.
newsitem.headline: Online bookstore war seen as Barnes & Noble enters.

text.p: Barnes & Noble Inc said its first site to sell books online is now live on America Online Inc, in its foray to sell books in cyberspace, a fast-growing market pioneered on the Internet by the startup Amazon.com.

In anticipation of the entry by the New York-based bookselling giant, Seattle-based Amazon.com on Monday said it was dropping its prices on all U.S. bestsellers and other books by up to 40 percent and it is expanding its book offerings to 2.5 million titles, up from 1.1 million titles previously.

Barnes & Noble said it will have a database of over one million book titles. It will launch its own Web site on the Internet this spring, which it said will incorporate several innovative bookselling techniques and new marketing partners.
Its online presence will begin in the AOL Marketplace section of the world's largest online service.

AOL has over eight million subscribers and Barnes & Noble will offer them immediate delivery on over 400,000 titles in stock at discounts of 30 percent for hardcovers and 20 percent for paperbacks. Special orders for books not in stock will be ordered from more than 20,000 publishers.

Barnes & Noble said its site on AOL has numerous features such as detailed book reviews, text excerpts and author information, top 10 lists and editors' picks. When it starts its own site on the Internet it will include several innovative bookselling techniques, Barnes & Noble said.

Amazon.com, which was founded in 1994 by Jeff Bezos, a former Wall Street executive, has become one of the most successful businesses on the Internet, selling books online with low overhead and an increasingly huge customer database.
The size of the Amazon.com catalog is about 14 times the size of the largest physical book superstore, Amazon said.

"Barnes & Noble has been notably slow in coming to market against the meteoric rise of Amazon.com, so it's not surprising that they are coming out with their guns blazing," said Adam Schoenfeld, an analyst at Jupiter Communications.

Schoenfeld said that he believes Amazon.com's brand name and its lower overhead will help it maintain a significant position in an increasingly bloody battle with the bookstore giants. Borders Group Inc of Ann Arbor, Mich. is also expected to jump into the online world soon.
"I expect (Amazon.com) to go all out against the encroachment of the bricks and mortar booksellers," he added.

These giant book merchants have higher costs because of their mammoth retail locations, and they are also at risk of cannibalizing their bookstore sales by online sales. But analysts said these new entrants will definitely have an impact on Amazon.com, which has had the market to itself.
"Just because they started late doesn't mean they won't do well," Schoenfeld said of the book retailers. "But Amazon.com is not a trifling startup, it's a serious venture."
Ted Julian, an International Data Corp analyst, said that teaming up with AOL was a smart move for Barnes & Noble, giving them access to a well-established online community.
